PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

1. Blood

Blood components:

  • Liquid (55%)
  • Solid (45%)
  • RBC, WBC, Platelets

Liquid portion → Plasma:

  • 92%: Water
  • 8%: Protein, Salt, Hormones

Liquid Part of Blood

Plasma

  • It is the yellow in color.
  • It consists of 92% water and 8% proteins, salt and hormones.
ProteinsFunction
Fibrinogen / HeparinAnticoagulants
GlobulinProvides defence
AlbuminTo maintain osmotic balance
When clotting proteins are removed from blood, the clear liquid that remains after is called Serum.

Solid Part of Blood

RBC (Red Blood Cells)/Erythrocytes

  • Normal range: 4.5 to 5.5 million per cubic millimeter.
  • Color: Red in color due to presence of heme (Fe). Heme has high affinity towards oxygen.
  • Shape: Biconcave; disc-shaped.
  • Lifespan and Formation: Bone marrow (at birth) having a lifespan of about 120 days.
  • Function: It transports oxygen to whole body.
  • Mature RBC's have no nucleus in them.
  • Graveyard of RBC: Spleen.

Study of Blood: Hematology

WBC (White Blood Cells)/Leukocytes

  • Normal range: 5000-8000 per cubic millimeter.
  • WBC's protects our body from infection (provides our body a defence mechanism).
  • Formed in: Bone marrow having life span of 13-20 days.
  • Shape: Round / Irregular in shape.
  • Types: Monocytes, Lymphocytes, Neutrophils, Basophils, Eosinophils.

Platelets/Thrombocytes

  • Normal range: 1,50,000-3,50,000 per cubic millimeter of blood.
  • Shape: Irregular shape.
  • Formed in: Bone marrow having life span of a 7-10 days.
  • Function: They are essential for preventing and stopping bleeding by forming coagulation.
  • Low platelet count leads to thrombocytopenia (happens in case of dengue) and a very high platelet count leads to called thrombocytosis.

2. Lymph

Structure:

  • It is a colorless fluid.
  • RBC and blood proteins are absent in lymph.
  • Lymph is similar to blood plasma → contains proteins, salt, glucose, and water.
  • It is slightly yellow in color.

Function:

  • Lymph plays a crucial role in maintaining bodily fluid balance and supporting the immune system.

Nervous Tissue

  • Neural tissue (or nervous tissue) is a specialized tissue found in the nervous system.
  • It is responsible for receiving stimuli, transmitting signals, and coordinating responses throughout the body.
  • Occurrence: Found in Brain, Spinal cord, Nerves.

Anatomy of a Neuron

  • A neuron is the basic structural and fundamental unit of the nervous system. It is specialized to transmit nerve impulses.
  • Neuron is the longest cell in the human body.

Parts of Neurons:

  1. 1. Cell Body (Soma)
  • It contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and controls the activities of the neuron.
  1. 2. Dendrites
  • Short, branched extensions from the cell body that receives signals from other neurons or sensory cells.
  • It carries impulses toward the cell body.
  1. 3. Axon
  • It carries nerve impulses away from the cell body to other neurons or

PLANT TISSUE AND ANIMAL TISSUE

effectors (muscles/glands)

  1. 4. Myelin Sheath
  • A fatty layer that covers the axon that insulates the axon and speeds up signal transmission.
  1. 5. Schwann Cells
  • They are glial cells that form the Myelin Sheath on Axons is outside the brain.
  1. 6. Axon Terminals (Synaptic knobs)
  • The end branches of the axon that contain neurotransmitters.
  • It helps transmit signals to the next neuron or effector cell across a synapse.

PLANT TISSUE

---

Transmission of Neuron Impulses

  • A stimulus is received by the dendrites.
  • An electrical impulse travels through the cell body and axon.
  • At the axon terminals, the impulse triggers the release of neurotransmitters.
  • Neurotransmitters cross the synapse and pass the signal to the next neuron or effector (like a muscle or gland).
  • This leads to a response.

How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?

Diagram shows: axon of previous neuron, neuron cell body, nucleus, axon tips, dendrites of next neuron, electrical signal, synapse.

One neuron's axon transmit information to other neuron's dendrite. The gap between these two is called synapse.

Camillo Golgi: First created the illustration of neuron using his silver-staining technique (Black Reaction).

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

CLASSIFICATION OF KINGDOM

Taxonomy

  • It is the science of describing, naming, and classifying organisms, including all plants, animals, and microorganisms.

Order of Classification

  • Kingdom Animalia → KABADDI
  • Phylum Chordata → PLAY
  • Class Mammalia → CLASS
  • Order Carnivora → OUR
  • Family Canidae → OF
  • Genus Vulpes → GIRLS
  • Species Vulpes vulpes → SOME
Some Girls Of Our Class Play Kabaddi.

Classification

Two Kingdom Classification

  • Proposed by: Carolus Linnaeus (1758) → "Father of Taxonomy".
  • Kingdoms:
  • → Plantae: Included all plants, algae, fungi.
  • → Animalia: Included all animals.
Linnaeus published "System Nature" in 1735.

Three Kingdom Classification

  • Proposed by: Ernst Haeckel (1866) → Coined the term "Ecology".
  • Kingdoms:
  • → Plantae
  • → Animalia
  • → Protista: New kingdom added for unicellular organisms (Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena).

Three Domain Classification

  • Proposed by: Carl Woese (1990).
  • Domains:
  • → Bacteria: True prokaryotes (E.g. E. coli).
  • → Archaea: Microorganisms with prokaryotic cells that are distinct from bacteria and are often found in extreme environments (E.g. Halobacterium).
  • → Eukarya: All eukaryotic organisms (Protists, Fungi, Plants, Animals).

Five Kingdom Classification

  • Proposed by: R.H. Whittaker (1969).
  • Kingdoms:
  • → Monera: Prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae).
  • → Protista: Eukaryotic unicellular organisms.
  • → Fungi: Eukaryotic multicellular (some are unicellular) organisms, heterotrophic, spore-producing organisms.
  • → Plantae: Autotrophic, multicellular.
  • → Animalia: Heterotrophic, multicellular.
  • Basis of classification: Cell structure, mode of nutrition, body organization, reproduction.

---

Types of Classification

  • Cell Nature: Prokaryotes / Eukaryotes
  • Cell Occurrence: Unicellular / Multicellular
  • Mode of Nutrition: Autotrophs / Heterotrophs
  • Level of Body Organization: Cellular / Tissue / Organ / Organ System

KINGDOM MONERA

  • Cell type: Prokaryotic (no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles).
  • Organization: Unicellular, microscopic.
  • Cell Wall: Made up of peptidoglycan (in bacteria).
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic) or heterotrophic (saprophytic or parasitic).

Classification of Kingdom Monera

Monera is mainly divided into two major groups:

  1. 1. Eubacteria (True bacteria)
  • Most common and well-known group of bacteria.
  • Cell wall: Contains peptidoglycan.
  • Nutrition: Mostly heterotrophic (saprophytes, parasites), with some autotrophs (including photoautotrophs like cyanobacteria).
  1. 2. Archaebacteria (Ancient bacteria)
  • They live in extreme environments (hot springs, salt lakes, swamps).
  • Cell wall: Cell wall present but lacks peptidoglycan.

KINGDOM PROTISTA

  • Cell type: Eukaryotic (has a true nucleus and organelles), cell wall is absent.
  • Organization: Mostly unicellular, some are colonial or simple multicellular.
  • Locomotion: Through appendages.
  • Nutrition:
  • → Autotrophic (photosynthesis): Algae.
  • → Heterotrophic: Protozoans (ingest food).
Habit: Growth form of a plant comprising its shape, size and orientation.
Habitat: Natural home or environment of a plant or animal.

Classification of Kingdom Protista

  1. 1. Phylum Protozoa
  • Cell type: Unicellular.
  • Mode of Nutrition: Heterotrophic (ingest food), parasitic or symbiotic.
  • Habitat: Mostly aquatic, solitary however few are colonial.
  • E.g. Euglena (uses flagellum for movement), Amoeba (uses pseudopodia, a false-feet for movement), Paramecium (uses cilia for movement, that also helps to move food to its oral cavity), Plasmodium.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

KINGDOM FUNGI

  • Cell Type: Eukaryotic (has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
  • Organization: Mostly multicellular, but some are unicellular (E.g. Yeast).
  • Cell Wall: Present and is made of chitin (not cellulose like in plants).
  • Nutrition: Heterotrophic, typically saprophytic (feed on decaying organic matter), but some are parasitic (dependent on protoplasm of a host organism for food or mutualistic (both benefits from their association and sharing of resources).
  • Some of them are in symbiotic relationship (benefit from each other). E.g. Lichen (Blue-green algae + Fungi). The fungus provides shelter, protection, and access to water and nutrients, while the blue-green algae (or green algae) produce food for the fungus through photosynthesis.

KINGDOM PLANTAE

  • Cell Type: Eukaryotic (has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
  • Organization: Multicellular.
  • Cell Wall: Made up of cellulose (provides structure and support).
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic (producing their own food via photosynthesis, using chlorophyll).

Kingdom Plantae is classified on the basis of:

  • Differentiation of plant body and distinct components.
  • Presence or absence of vascular tissues.
  • Ability to bear seeds.
  • Seeds are enclosed within the fruits.
  • Ability to produce flowers.

Cryptogamae Vs Phanerogamae

CryptogamaePhanerogamae
Seeds, fruits, flowers are absent.Seeds, fruits, flowers are present.
Reproductive organs are hidden.Reproductive organs are exposed.
Less evolved plantsHighly evolved plants
E.g. Thallophytes, Bryophytes, and PteridophytesE.g. Gymnosperms and Angiosperms

Phylums of Kingdom Plantae

Phycology: Study of Algae
  1. 1. Thallophyta (Algae)
  • Cell type: Eukaryotic.
  • Simple, do not have well-differentiated body parts such as roots or stem (they have thallus).
  • Non-vascular (no specialized tissue for transporting water and nutrients).
  • Habitat: Mostly aquatic, mostly found in freshwater or marine environments. E.g. Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Ulva, Chara.
  • Movement: Non-motile.
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic, photosynthetic (contain chlorophyll). Different pigments are present (edible or non-edible).
  • E.g.
  • Chlorophyceae (Green algae): Chlorella (rich in proteins), Spirulina (superfood).
  • Phaeophyceae (Brown algae): Sargassum, Laminaria (Kelp).
  • Rhodophyceae (Red algae): Gelidium, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Polysiphonia.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

  • Agar a jelly like substance, is obtained from Rhodophyceae (red algae).
  1. 2. Bryophyta (Bryophytes)
  • They are known as "Amphibians of plant kingdom" (exists both in land and water).
  • Non-vascular plants → no specialised tissues for water and food conduction (lack xylem and phloem).
  • They have well-differentiated body however lack true roots, stems and leaves. Roots like structure present in bryophytes are called Rhizoids.
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic.
  • Movement: Non-motile.
  • Reproduction: Through spores (no seeds) in water.
  • → Male reproductive part: Antheridium.
  • → Female reproductive part: Archegonium.
  • Habitat: Found in damp and moist areas.
  • E.g.
  • Mosses: Funaria.
  • Liverworts: Marchantia, Riccia.

Diagram: Sporophyte (Diploid) → Capsule, Stalk (Seta); Gametophyte (body with "leaves"), Gametophyte (Haploid) → Rhizoid

  1. 3. Phylum Pteridophyta
  • They are considered as first terrestrial vascular plants (have xylem and phloem).
  • Well-differentiated roots, stems, and leaves (called fronds in ferns). Leaves are made of leaflets that bear spores called Sporophylls.
  • They have hidden reproductive organs (cryptogams).
  • Habitat: Found in cracks of rocks, moist, and shady places.
  • E.g. Marsilea, Ferns, and Horsetails.

The Parts of a Fern — Fiddle, Frond, Blade, Pinna, Pinnule, Rhizome, Root, Sori

---

Gymnosperms (Meaning: Gymno (without cover) and Sperma (seeds without fruits))

  • Vascular plants, have true roots, stem and leaves (with xylem and phloem).
  • Phloem Companion and Xylem Vessel are absent.
  • Seed-producing plants, but seeds are naked (not enclosed in fruit). The seeds are primitive and simple.
  • They are usually perennials, evergreen, and mostly woody plants.
  • E.g. Pines, Deodar, Cycas.

Angiosperms (Meaning: Angio (covered) and Sperma (seeds))

  • They are flowering plants and produce seeds enclosed within fruit (ovary gets modified into fruit).
  • Vascular plants with xylem and phloem. They are highly evolved.
  • Flowers are the reproductive organs.
  • Seeds have embryo inside it and embryos have structure called cotyledons (seed leaves).

Diverse group, with two major classes:

  • → Monocots: They have one cotyledon. E.g., grasses, lilies.
  • → Dicots: They have two cotyledons. E.g., roses, sunflowers.

Monocot vs Dicot

Monocots and dicots are the two broad groups of flowering plants.

  • Monocots: 1 cotyledon, fibrous roots, parallel leaf veins, scattered stem vascular bundles, flower parts in threes.
  • Dicots: 2 cotyledons, tap root, net leaf veins, vascular bundles form ring, flower parts in fours or fives.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

Remember: Main plant body in Algae and Bryophytes is Gametophyte (n) while in Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms, and Angiosperms, it is Sporophyte (2n).

KINGDOM ANIMALIA

Kingdom Animalia classification tree:

  • Invertebrates (without backbone): Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata
  • Vertebrates (with backbone): Fish, Reptiles, Amphibians, Birds, Mammals

Let's first classify them under certain Parameters!

Kingdom Animalia

  • They are eukaryotic and multicellular organisms.
  • They are heterotrophic.
  • Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall.
  • Mobility: Most animals are capable of movement at some stage of their life cycle.
  • Kingdom Animalia is classified into phylum on the basis of extent and type of body design differentiation found in them.

---

Body Level Organisation

  • Body level organization refers to the hierarchical arrangement of structures within a living organism, from the smallest units to the entire organism. It involves five main levels: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and the organism.

Diagram: cell → tissue → organ → organ system

On the Basis of Symmetry

  • Asymmetrical: Asymmetry refers to the lack of symmetry in an organism's body plan. E.g. Porifera.
  • Radial Symmetry: In radial symmetry, any plane passing through the central axis divides the organism into two equal halves. E.g. Coelenterata, Echinodermata.
  • Bilateral Symmetry: Bilateral symmetry is characterized by a single plane of symmetry that divides the organism into left and right halves. E.g. Platyhelminthes, Arthropoda.

Symmetry diagram: No Symmetry (e.g. Porifera), Radial Symmetry (e.g. Cnidaria), Bilateral Symmetry (e.g. Annelids)

On the Basis of Germ Layers

  • Diploblastic: Animals with only two germ layers: Ectoderm (outermost germ layer) and Endoderm (innermost germ layer).
  • Triploblastic: Animals with three germ layers: Ectoderm, Mesoderm (middle germ layer), Endoderm. E.g. Porifera, Coelenterate and Ctenophora are Diploblastic and rest all are Triploblastic.

Diagram: Diploblastic vs Triploblastic — Mesoglea, Ectoderm, Endoderm

On the Basis of Coelom

  • → Coelom: It is the body cavity present between the body wall, and the gut wall. Coelom has a mesodermal lining.
  • Acoelomate: No coelom. E.g. Porifera, Coelenterate, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes.
  • Pseudocoelomate: False coelom. E.g. Nematoda.
  • Eucoelomate: True coelom. E.g. Annelida, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Chordata.

Coelom diagram: Acoelomate (Perform Coelenterata), Pseudo-Coelom (Aschelminthes/Nematoda), True Coelom (Annelida to Chordata) — Ectoderm, Endoderm, Mesoderm, Pseudocoelom, Coelom

On the Basis of Circulatory System

  • Open Circulatory System: It is a system where there is no vessel to contain the blood and it flows freely through the cavities of the body. E.g. Arthropoda, Mollusca.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

Body segmentation refers to the division of an animal's body into repeating, similar units called segments. E.g. Seen in: Annelida, Arthropoda, Chordata.

  • Closed Circulatory System: It is a system where the blood is always contained within vessels in the heart while circulating. E.g. Annelida, Chordata.

Notochord

  • The notochord is a rod-like structure made of a cartilaginous substance that develops in all chordates at early embryonic stages as a rudimentary backbone.
  • It is derived from mesoderm.
  • It is present in the dorsal side (upper side or back side of an animal). E.g. Chordata.

1. Phylum Porifera

  • Habitat: Mostly aquatic, marine, and a few freshwater species (E.g. Spongilla).
  • Body symmetry: Asymmetrical.
  • Body structure: Body is perforated with many tiny holes or pores (Ostium: Water canal system). Pores lead to a large central cavity called the Spongocoel. They have specialized "collar cells".
  • Level of organization: Cellular level organization (no true tissues or organs).
  • Germ layer: Diploblastic (endoderm and ectoderm).
  • Movement: Non-motile.
  • Endoskeleton is present.
  • They are hermaphrodites (posses both male and female reproductive system).

2. Phylum Coelenterata/Cnidaria

  • Habitat: Aquatic, mostly marine, a few freshwater species (E.g. Hydra).
  • Symmetry: Radial symmetry.
  • Level of organization: Tissue level organization.
  • Germ layers: Diploblastic.
  • Body structure: Sac-like body with a central gastrovascular cavity (E.g. Coral, Hydra) having only one opening (hypostome) that serves as both mouth and anus. Tentacles surround the mouth, used for capturing food.
  • Special cells: Stinging cells called Cnidoblast contain a stinging capsule known as Nematocyst.
  • Hard skeleton is developed outside the body called Exoskeleton (made of calcium carbonate). E.g. Jellyfish, Aurelia.

3. Phylum Ctenophora

  • Habitat: Exclusively marine.
  • They exhibit bioluminescence.
  • Body symmetry: Radial symmetry.
  • They are also known as Sea Walnuts and Comb Jellies.
  • Reproduction: Sexual reproduction. They are hermaphrodites.
  • E.g. Pleurobrachia and Ctenoplana.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

4. Phylum Platyhelminthes

  • Body shape: Body is dorsoventrally flattened like a ribbon (flat from top to bottom). Suckers and hooks are present in few.
  • Habitat and nature: They are either free living or parasitic and terrestrial. E.g. Planaria (free-living), Liverfluke (parasitic), Tapeworm.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral symmetry.
  • Germ layers: Triploblastic.
  • Level of organization: Organ level of organization (more advanced than Porifera and Coelenterata).
  • Coelom: Acoelomate.
  • Digestive system: Incomplete digestive system (common opening for both mouth and anus). Anus is absent.
  • Excretory system: Excretion and osmoregulation through specialized cells called flame cells.
  • They are hermaphrodites.

5. Phylum Aschelminthes/Nematodes

  • Body shape: Cylindrical, elongated, unsegmented body, tapered at both ends (spindle-shaped).
  • Symmetry: Bilateral symmetry.
  • Germ layers: Triploblastic.
  • Level of organization: Organ level organization.
  • Coelom: Pseudocoelomate.
  • Habitat: Most forms are parasitic, but some are free living in soil or water.
  • Digestive system: Alimentary canal is complete (has both mouth and anus). Animals show sexual dimorphism (males and females look different). Mostly unisexual (male and female are separate).
  • Excretory system: Renette cells are present.
  • E.g. Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filarial worm), Ancyclostoma (hookworm).

6. Phylum Annelida

  • Body: Dorsoventrally flattened, cylindrical, segmentation is present on body.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
  • Germ layers: Triploblastic.
  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Level of organization: Organ system level.
  • Digestive System: Alimentary canal is tube like structure extended from mouth to anus.
  • Circulatory system: Closed (blood flows in vessels).
  • Locomotion: Through locomotory organs like parapodia (Nereis) that are lateral appendages.
  • Reproduction: Sexual, some are hermaphrodites, some show asexual reproduction.
  • Excretory system: Nephridia is present for osmoregulation and excretion.
  • E.g. Earthworms, Leech, Nereis, Hirudinaria, etc.

7. Phylum Arthropoda

  • Largest phylum in Animal Kingdom → Insecta is the largest class.
  • Body: Segmented into head, thorax, and abdomen. They have joint appendages (jointed legs).
  • Exoskeleton: Made of chitin.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
  • Coelom: True, filled with blood.
  • Habitat: Terrestrial, aquatic, fresh or marine animals.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • Circulatory System: Open circulatory system.
  • Respiration through: Gills, trachea, or book lungs.
  • Excretion through: Malpighian tubules.
  • Reproduction: Mostly unisexual, sexual dimorphism is common.
  • Digestive system: Alimentary canal is complete.
  • E.g. Spider, scorpio, crab, silver fish, cray fish, etc.

8. Phylum Mollusca

  • It is the second largest phylum of Animal Kingdom.
  • Body: Soft, little segmentation. The body is divided into head, foot, and a mantle (a fold of thin skin).
  • Covering: Most have a calcareous shell (snails).
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
Devil fish is common name of Octopus.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Circulatory System: Mostly open; closed in octopus and squid.
  • Respiration: Gills or lungs.
  • Digestive system: Alimentary canal is complete.
  • Excretory system: Kidney-like organs called nephridia is present for excretion.
  • Reproduction: Unisexual, external or internal fertilization.
  • They have blue color blood due to Haemocyanin.
  • E.g. Octopus, snails (pila), oysters, squid, etc.

9. Phylum Echinodermata

  • Body: Star-shaped, spherical, elongated. They are spiny-skinned organisms with no segmentation on body.
  • Symmetry: Radial.
  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • System of organization: Organ system. E.g. Sea urchins, starfish, Holothuria, sea cucumber.

10. Phylum Chordata

  • They have a notochord (rod-like supportive structure).
  • They have pharyngeal gill slits in pharynx.
  • Heart is ventral.
  • Circulatory system: Closed circulatory system.
  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • Level of organization: Organ level of organization.
  • Phylum Chordata is divided into two major groups: Protochordata and Vertebrata.
Remember: Hemichordata is not a sub-phylum under Chordata. It consists of small group of worm like animals.
Protochordata have notochord, but never form a verbal column.

---

Characteristics of Protochordata

  • They do not have proper notochord (present only in larval stage or not well developed).
  • No vertebral column, post anal tail present.
  • Bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate.
  • Nerve cord is present.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • Pharyngeal gill slits present.

Classes of Vertebrates

  1. 1. Cyclostomata
  • They are jawless vertebrates.
  • They have elongated eel-like body, circular mouth, and slimy skin.
  • E.g. Petromyzon/Myxine, hog fishes, lamprey.
  1. 2. Pisces
  • They are fishes. E.g Dog fish, shark, tuna, sea horse, etc.
  • Pieces have two-chambered heart.
  1. 3. Amphibians
  • They use mucous glands or gills for respiration.
  • They have three-chambered heart.
  • They are cold blooded animals.
  • They breathe through lungs or gills (in water) and skin (in land).
  • E.g. Frogs, toads, salamander.
  1. 4. Reptiles
  • They have three-chambered heart [exception: Crocodile (has four-chambered heart)].
  • They are cold blooded animals.
  • They breathe through their lungs.
  • E.g. Snake, turtle, lizard, crocodile, chameleon.
  1. 5. Aves (Birds)
  • They have four-chambered heart.
  • They are warm blooded.
  • They lay eggs (oviparous).
  1. 6. Mammals
  • They have four-chambered heart.
  • They are warm blooded.
  • They have mammary glands (viviparous). Exception: Platypus and echidnas (lay eggs).
  • E.g. Dolphin, whale, humans, etc.

NERVOUS SYSTEM

NERVOUS SYSTEM

  • The nervous system is a complex network of cells and nerves that controls and coordinates the body's functions. It includes the brain, spinal cord, and all the nerves that connect these organs to the rest of the body.

Diagram: Nervous System → Central Nervous System (Brain, Spinal Cord) and Peripheral Nervous System (Nerves emanating from Brain and Spinal Cord)

Central Nervous System

  • The central nervous system (CNS) is the body's primary control center, responsible for processing information and coordinating bodily functions. It's made up of the brain and the spinal cord.

Functions of CNS:

  • It collects signals from sense organs (eyes, ears, skin, etc.).
  • It sends signals to muscles and glands to respond appropriately.
  • It controls voluntary (walking, writing, speaking, etc.) and involuntary movements (heartbeat, digestion, etc.).
  • The CNS plays a crucial role in thermoregulation, the process of maintaining a stable body temperature.
  • The CNS specifically the hypothalamus, plays a crucial role in controlling both hunger and thirst.

Human Brain

  • The human brain is the main organ of the central nervous system (CNS).
  • It is protected by the skull and surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid.
  • It controls all body functions, including movement, emotions, thoughts, memory, and senses.
  • Inside the skull, the brain is covered by the cranial meninges.
  • Meninges consists of three layers:
  • Dura Mater: Outer layer.
  • Arachnoid Mater: A very thin middle layer.
  • Pia Mater: Inner layer (which is in contact with the brain tissue).
Pain receptors are present in meninges.
  • Total number of bones in skull: 22 → Facial bones (14) and Cranial bones (8).
The adult brain accounts for mere of 2% of body weight but consumes:
- 20%: O₂
- 20-25%: Glucose (our brain demands half of the sugar energy).

The human brain can be divided into three major parts:

  1. 1. Fore Brain
  • The "forebrain" refers to the anterior (front) part of the brain, and it's the largest section of the brain.
  • It controls all the voluntary movements and higher-level cognitive functions like thinking, memory, and consciousness.
  • Parts of Fore Brain: Cerebrum, Thalamus, Hypothalamus.

(a) Cerebrum

  • It is the largest part of the brain.
  • The left and right cerebral hemispheres are connected by a thick band of nerve fibers called the corpus callosum. (The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain; the cerebellum is the second-largest, located in the hindbrain.)
  • The outer layer of cell, which covers the cerebral hemisphere is called cerebral cortex (referred to as grey matter due to its greyish appearance).
  • Cerebrum is responsible for memory and learning.

(b) Thalamus (Pain and Sensation)

  • It is the major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signaling.
  • Thalamus works as a "Relay Station". It takes information from the body and sends it further to cerebral cortex (Body senses → Thalamus → Cerebral cortex).
  • Touch, taste, sound → these senses are processed by Thalamus to Cerebral Cortex.

(c) Hypothalamus

  • Hypothalamus lies at the base of thalamus.
  • It controls the Autonomic Nervous System and is required for regulating inner body temperature, eating, drinking and vomiting.
  • It contains several groups of neurosecretory cells, which secretes hormone called hypothalamic hormones.
  1. 2. Mid Brain
  • It is located between Hypothalamus of forebrain and pons of hindbrain.
  • It is involved in several functions such as: Motor control, particularly eye movements and processing of vision and hearing.
  1. 3. Hind Brain
  • Parts of Hind Brain: Pons, Cerebellum, Medulla Oblongata.

(a) Pons

  • It is the middle portion of the brain that coordinates face and eye movements, facial sensations, hearing and balance.

(b) Cerebellum

  • It maintains body posture and balance, and is also known as "little brain".

(c) Medulla Oblongata

  • It is connected to the spinal cord. It controls involuntary actions like respiration, heartbeat, and gastric secretions.

Lobes of the Brain

  • The brain is divided into four main lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital.
  1. 1. Frontal Lobe
  • Location: Front of the brain.
  • Functions: Reasoning, planning, problem-solving, motor control, emotional regulation.

NERVOUS SYSTEM

  1. 2. Parietal Lobe
  • Location: Behind the frontal lobe.
  • Functions: Processes sensory information (touch, pain, temperature), spatial awareness.
  1. 3. Temporal Lobe
  • Location: Sides of the brain.
  • Functions: Auditory processing, language comprehension, memory, emotions.
  1. 4. Occipital Lobe
  • Location: Back of the brain.
  • Functions: Visual processing, understanding spatial relationships.

Brain lobes diagram: Frontal Lobe, Parietal Lobe, Temporal Lobe, Occipital Lobe

Spinal Cord

  • The spinal cord transmits signals from the brain to the body and sensory information from the body back to the brain. It also plays a role in coordinating reflexes.

The Spinal Cord is divided into three sections:

  1. 1. Cervical: Neck.
  2. 2. Thoracic: Upper back.
  3. 3. Lumbar: Lower back.

Spinal cord sections & nerve groups:

  • Cervical (8 nerve pairs)
  • Thoracic (12 nerve pairs)
  • Lumbar (5 nerve pairs)
  • Sacral (5 nerve pairs)
  • Cauda equina
  • → There are a total of 31 pair of nerves connected to the spinal cord.
  • Cervical: 8 nerve pairs.
  • Thoracic: 12 nerve pairs.
  • Lumbar: 5 pairs of nerves.
  • Sacral: 5 pairs of nerves.

Spinal cord diagram: Spinal cord, Pia matter, Arachnoid matter, Dura mater

Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

  • The final nerve is a bundle at the base of spine called "cauda equina" that gives sensation to your lower body.

---

Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

  • The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is a network of nerves that extends from the CNS (brain and spinal cord) throughout the body, connecting it to all other parts.
  1. 1. Somatic Nervous System: The somatic nervous system is a part of the peripheral nervous system that controls voluntary movements of skeletal muscles and receives sensory information from the skin, muscles, and joints.

Types:

  • (a) Sensory Nervous System: They carry information from body organs to CNS. They are also known as Afferent Nerves.
  • (b) Motor Nervous System: They carry information from CNS to body organs. They are also known as Efferent Nerves.
  1. 2. Autonomic Nervous System: The autonomic nervous system is a part of the peripheral nervous system that regulates involuntary physiologic processes including heart rate, blood pressure, respiration, digestion, and sexual arousal.

Types:

  • (a) Sympathetic Nervous System: They control the body's "Flight-or-Fight" response (help you in times of need, such as danger or stress).
  • (b) Parasympathetic Nervous System: They control the body's "Rest and Digest" response (It relaxes the body's system and return them to normal).

Pathway to Peripheral Nervous System

Diagram: Spinal cord (CNS), Message to brain, Sensory neuron, Motor neuron, Relay neuron, Receptors = Heat/Pain, Receptors in skin, Effector = Muscle in arm — showing reflex arc

  • Pathway: Stimulus (Heat) → Receptors → Sensory Neuron → Spinal Cord (Relay Neuron) → Motor Neuron → Muscle (Effector) → Response (Hand moves away)

Brain Diseases

  1. 1. Meningitis: Meningitis is a serious medical condition where the protective membranes (called meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord become inflamed.
  1. 2. Alzheimer's Disease: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive brain disorder that slowly destroys memory, thinking skills, and the ability to carry out simple tasks. It is the most common cause of dementia (loss of memory) in older adults.

NERVOUS SYSTEM

  1. 3. Amnesia: Amnesia is a condition where a person loses their memory, either partially or completely. It affects a person's ability to remember past experiences or form new memories.

HORMONES AND PLANT MOVEMENTS

GLANDS AND HORMONES

  • Glands are organs in the body that produce and release substances, either hormones or other chemicals, to perform specific functions.
  • Types of glands: Endocrine Glands and Exocrine Glands.
Endocrine GlandsExocrine Glands
They release hormonesThey release enzymes
They release hormones directly into the bloodThey secrete their enzymes using a duct
They are ductless glandsThey have ducts
- Hormones discovered by: E. H. Starling.
- 1st hormone discovered: Secretin (1902).

Major Endocrine Glands

Pituitary Gland

  • It is also known as the "master gland", this pea-sized gland is located at the base of the brain.
  • It produces hormones that regulate other endocrine glands, including growth hormone, prolactin, and oxytocin.
  • The pituitary gland is controlled by hypothalamus.

Hypothalamus

  • The hypothalamus is a brain region crucial for regulating many bodily functions, including hormone release, body temperature, hunger, and sleep-wake cycles.
  • The hypothalamus is responsible for regulating the secretion of hormones, and the pituitary gland releases these hormones into the bloodstream.

Pituitary Regions

  1. 1. Anterior Pituitary (Adenohypophysis): The anterior pituitary produces and secretes a variety of hormones that regulate various physiological processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress response.

Hormones released:

  • (a) Growth Hormone (Somatotropin): GHRH (Growth hormone-releasing hormone) releases growth hormones in anterior pituitary.
  • (b) Prolactin: It is involved in formation of milk.
  • Deficiency of GH leads to: Dwarfism (shortness in height due to genetic or medical condition).
  • Excess of GH causes: Gigantism (excessive growth and abnormal skeletal development), Acromegaly (result in excess growth of certain parts of human body).
  1. 2. Posterior Pituitary (Neurohypophysis): The posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones produced by the hypothalamus, but does not produce hormones itself.

Hormones released:

  • (a) ADH (Antidiuretic hormone/Vasopressin): It regulates the amount of water (reabsorption of H₂O), helps control blood pressure).
  • (b) Oxytocin (Love hormone): Involved in secretion of milk and stimulates the uterine muscle to contract during labour.

Pineal Gland

  • The pineal gland is a tiny endocrine gland in the middle of our brain that helps regulate body's circadian rhythm by secreting the hormone melatonin.
Melatonin is a hormone secreted by the pineal gland in response to darkness, often called the "hormone of darkness". It helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle by sensing light and dark through signals received from the retina of the eye.

Thymus

  • Located in the upper chest, behind the sternum (breastbone) and in front of the heart.
  • It plays a crucial role in the immune system, especially during childhood.
  • It responsible for the maturation of T-lymphocytes (T-cells), which are essential for fighting infections.
Serotonin hormone regulates moods and feelings.

Thyroid Gland

  • The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland located in the neck.
  • It produces a hormone called thyroxine, which plays a vital role in increasing the body's metabolism.
  • The production of thyroxine requires iodine, a mineral obtained from our diet.
  • A deficiency of iodine can lead to hypothyroidism, a condition where the body doesn't produce enough thyroid hormone.
